sections.b: Job's prologue tells the reader what no one in the story learns: Job suffers not for any sin but because the Accuser asks whether he fears God "for no reason" (Job 1:9), and the LORD allows a test within strict limits (Job 1:12; 2:6). The LORD himself says the Accuser lured him to swallow Job up "for no reason" (Job 2:3). So the book's first word on suffering is that it can have a cause hidden from the sufferer and unrelated to his guilt. It does not say every sufferer is being tested; it shows that the friends' rule, suffering means sin, cannot be applied to this man. Job's first responses, blessing the LORD who gave and took (Job 1:21) and taking the bad with the good (Job 2:10), are the patient faith of James 5:11; his laments in chapters 3 and 7 are the other half of the same faith.

sections.h: Their arrival and Eliphaz's first speech (Job 2:11–5:27)
sections.b: The friends enter well. Hearing of Job's trouble, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite arrange to come and "shake their heads with him and comfort him" (Job 2:11). They do not recognize him, weep, tear their robes and sit with him seven days and nights without a word (Job 2:12–13). Eliphaz, probably the eldest, speaks first and with courtesy (Job 4:2–6), but his teaching sets the pattern for all three: the innocent never perish (Job 4:7), a night voice told him no mortal is pure before God (Job 4:17), and Job should seek God and welcome his discipline, which will restore him (Job 5:8, 17–26). Job replies that his friends have failed him like a dry desert stream (Job 6:15–21).

sections.h: The man of Uz and his test (Job 1–2)
sections.b: The book introduces Job as a man of Uz, outside Israel, who was wholehearted and upright, feared God and kept away from evil (Job 1:1), the greatest man of the East (Job 1:3). The LORD himself calls him "my servant" and says there is no one like him on earth (Job 1:8; 2:3). When the Accuser asks whether Job fears God "for no reason" (Job 1:9), Job is stripped of his herds, his servants, his ten children and his health. His first answers are famous: "The LORD gave, and the LORD took. Let the LORD's name be blessed" (Job 1:21), and "Should we take the good from God, and not take the bad too?" (Job 2:10). This is the patient Job of James 5:11.

After seven silent days Job curses the day of his birth (Job 3:1–10), longs for the rest of the dead (Job 3:11–19), and asks why life is given to the miserable (Job 3:20–26). Answering Eliphaz, he says his friends have failed him like a dry desert stream (Job 6:15–20), and then turns to God himself: "Am I the Sea, or am I the Dragon, that you station a guard over me?" (Job 7:12). His bitter retelling of Psalm 8 (Job 7:17–18) and his plea for forgiveness before he dies (Job 7:21) show a man who argues with God because he cannot let God go.

common: Job is the Bible's model of patience, because of James 5:11 and his first responses in Job 1:21 and 2:10.
uncommon: Some readers, ancient and modern, argue that Job never existed and that the book is a parable, a view already recorded in the Talmud (Bava Batra 15a).

sections.b: In Job 1–2 ha-satan, "the Accuser," comes among the sons of God when they take their stand before the LORD (Job 1:6; 2:1). He has been roaming the earth (Job 1:7), questions whether Job's piety is "for no reason" (Job 1:9), and twice receives limited power to strike Job (Job 1:12; 2:6). The article shows that this is a title, not a name. Readers disagree whether he is a loyal prosecutor of the heavenly court, as many Jewish readers and modern scholars hold, or the devil, God's enemy, as most Christian readers have taken him. The Old Greek calls him ho diabolos. He disappears after Job 2:7, and the LORD's speeches never mention him.

common: The Satan of Job is the devil, who tests Job out of malice, as most Christian readers have held.
uncommon: The Accuser of Job is a loyal servant of God who 'acted for the sake of heaven', as the Talmud says (Bava Batra 16a).

sections.h: The sons of God before the LORD (Job 1–2; 5:1)
sections.b: Job's prologue opens twice in the heavenly court: "the sons of God came and took their stand before the LORD" (Job 1:6; 2:1), and the LORD questions the Accuser, who reports on his travels. The scene is like 1 Kings 22:19–22, where the LORD consults his host. The Old Greek renders "the angels of God." Eliphaz later mentions the "holy ones" (Job 5:1) and says God finds error even in his messengers (Job 4:18), and the sons of God shout for joy at creation (Job 38:7).

sections.h: Eliphaz's rule and the case it cannot explain (Job 4–5)
sections.b: Eliphaz states the doctrine of reward and punishment as a law of experience: "has an innocent man ever been lost?" (Job 4:7); whoever plows wickedness reaps it (Job 4:8). He softens it with the hope of discipline: "Think how fortunate a man is when God corrects him!" (Job 5:17), promising Job restored safety, children and long life (Job 5:18–26). The reader already knows from the prologue that Job's suffering is not punishment and not correction, but a test (Job 1:9–12; 2:3). The book sets the teaching of Proverbs and Deuteronomy beside a case it does not fit, and the LORD's verdict that the friends did not speak rightly (Job 42:7) shows that the rule cannot be applied in reverse, from suffering to sin.

common: Job's friends were wrong because they taught that God rewards the good and punishes the wicked.
uncommon: The friends' theology was largely right; their fault was applying a general truth to a particular man without evidence, as Clines and others argue.

sections.h: The wise man of the East (Job 1:1–3)
sections.b: Job is introduced in the words of Israel's wisdom motto: he "feared God and kept away from evil" (Job 1:1; compare Proverbs 3:7; Job 28:28), and he is the greatest of the people of the East, a region famed for its sages (Job 1:3; 1 Kings 4:30). His friends come from places of wisdom, Eliphaz from Teman (Job 2:11; Jeremiah 49:7). Eliphaz speaks as the voice of tested tradition, "We have studied it, and that is how it is" (Job 5:27). The book uses the wisdom tradition's own language to test that tradition.

Job 3 is one of the Bible's darkest laments: Job curses the day of his birth (Job 3:3–10), as Jeremiah does (Jeremiah 20:14–18), asks why he did not die at birth (Job 3:11–19) and why light is given to the miserable (Job 3:20–26). In Job 7 the lament becomes a prayer of complaint addressed to God (Job 7:7–21), with the psalmists' themes of life's brevity (Psalm 39; Psalm 90), sleepless nights (Psalm 6:6) and the cry "How long?" (Job 7:19). God rebukes the friends, not the lamenter (Job 42:7).

sections.h: The quiet of the dead and no return (Job 3; 7)
sections.b: In Job 3:13–19 the world of the dead is a place of rest where kings and stillborn babies lie together, the wicked stop their turmoil and the slave is free of his master. In Job 7:9–10 Sheol is a place of no return: "A cloud thins out and goes away; just so, the one who goes down to Sheol never climbs back up." The rabbis read 7:9 as Job's denial of the resurrection (Bavli Bava Batra 16a); later chapters raise the question again (Job 14:13–14; 19:25–27).

sections.h: Leviathan roused and the Dragon guarded (Job 3:8; 7:12)
sections.b: Job twice draws on the old pictures of chaos. He calls on "those who are ready to wake Leviathan" to curse the day of his birth (Job 3:8), and he asks God, "Am I the Sea, or am I the Dragon, that you station a guard over me?" (Job 7:12), recalling the stories in which Baal defeats Yam and Anat muzzles the dragon, and Marduk sets a guard over the waters of Tiamat. The LORD's speeches later describe how he shut in the sea (Job 38:8–11) and masters Leviathan (Job 41).

Job uses the name YHWH, "the LORD," in the prose story (Job 1–2; 42) and the speeches from the storm (Job 38:1; 40:1–6), but almost never in the debate, where Job and his friends, men of the East, say El, Eloah and Shaddai, "the Almighty" (Job 3:4; 5:17; 6:4). Eloah, the singular of Elohim, occurs more than forty times in Job and rarely elsewhere; Shaddai, the patriarchs' name for God (Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3), appears 31 times. The narrator lets the reader know that the God they argue about is the LORD.

sections.h: Loyal love owed to the despairing (Job 6:14)
sections.b: Job's complaint against his friends turns on hesed: "A man who is melting away should have loyal love from his friend, even if he gives up the fear of the Almighty" (Job 6:14). The line is hard and has other readings, but on the most common one Job says that friendship's loyalty does not depend on the sufferer's piety. He compares his friends to a desert stream that fails the caravans (Job 6:15–20).

Job's curse runs creation in reverse. "That day: let there be darkness!" (Job 3:4) answers "Let there be light" (Genesis 1:3); he asks that the day not be counted among the days and months (Job 3:6; compare Genesis 1:14) and calls on those who rouse Leviathan (Job 3:8). Michael Fishbane argued that the poem takes up the days of creation one by one to undo them, as Jeremiah 4:23–26 does. The LORD's answer from the storm returns to the founding of the earth and the morning stars (Job 38:4–12).

Job wishes he had died at birth (Job 3:11), envies those who find the grave (Job 3:21–22), asks God to crush him and cut him off (Job 6:8–9), and says he would rather be strangled (Job 7:15). Yet he never considers taking his own life; he asks God to end it. Readers often place him with Moses, Elijah and Jonah, who asked God to let them die (Numbers 11:15; 1 Kings 19:4; Jonah 4:3), and the Talmud's principle that a person is not held responsible for words spoken in distress (Bavli Bava Batra 16b) is often applied to him.

sections.h: Uz and Teman: Job's eastern world (Job 1:1; 2:11)
sections.b: Job lives in Uz, which Lamentations 4:21 links with Edom, and his friend Eliphaz comes from Teman, an Edomite town famous for wisdom (Job 2:11; Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 8–9). Eliphaz and Teman are also names in Esau's family (Genesis 36:4, 11). The Greek ending of Job identifies Job with Jobab, a king of Edom (Genesis 36:33). Israel's greatest book on suffering is set among its eastern neighbors.
sections.refs: Job 1:1; Job 2:11; Lamentations 4:21; Genesis 36:4; Genesis 36:11; Genesis 36:33; Jeremiah 49:7

sections.b: Job's first words to God are worship in loss: "The LORD gave, and the LORD took. Let the LORD's name be blessed" (Job 1:21). His first extended prayer is a complaint (Job 7:7–21): remember that my life is wind; why have you made me your target; why not forgive me? The friends talk about God; Job talks to him, and the LORD in the end says Job spoke rightly (Job 42:7).

Job's disease is described in the words of the covenant curse: "bad boils from the soles of his feet to his scalp" (Job 2:7; compare Deuteronomy 28:35). To any Israelite, Job looks like a man under God's curse, which is just what his friends conclude. The reader knows otherwise. The book also plays on blessing and cursing: the Hebrew writes "bless" for "curse" in Job 1:5, 1:11, 2:5 and 2:9, the question being whether Job will bless God or curse him.

sections.h: Job and the righteous sufferers of Babylon and Egypt (Job 1–7)
sections.b: Job's story has relatives. The Babylonian Ludlul bel nemeqi ("I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom") tells of a devout man struck by illness and abandoned, whose god Marduk finally restores him; the Babylonian Theodicy is a dialogue between a sufferer and a friend; the Sumerian "A Man and His God" counsels confession; the Egyptian "Dispute of a Man with His Ba" longs for death. Job shares their laments and nights of pain (Job 7:3–5), their Resheph and chaos monsters (Job 5:7; 7:12), but its prologue tells the reader what none of them say: this sufferer is innocent, and his suffering is a test.

Eliphaz's counsel is to seek God: "If it were me, I would turn to God, and leave my case with God" (Job 5:8), followed by a hymn to God's great deeds (Job 5:9–16). Job will take the advice in his own way, not by submitting but by seeking a hearing for his case (Job 13:3; 23:3–7), and the LORD answers him (Job 38:1).

Job acts as priest for his family, offering burnt offerings early in the morning, one for each child, in case they have sinned and cursed God in their hearts (Job 1:5). With no priest, temple or altar named, the scene recalls the patriarchs (Genesis 8:20; 22:13), and at the end Job offers for his friends at the LORD's command (Job 42:8).

Before Job hopes for a go'el (Job 19:25), he uses the verb in a dark sense: let darkness and deep shadow "reclaim" the day of his birth, as a kinsman reclaims family property (Job 3:5; compare Leviticus 25:25). In Job 6:23 he says he never asked his friends to "buy me back" (padah) from tyrants. The language of redemption is present from the start, waiting for its turn.
